chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by late dialogic framing and institutional/pastoral instruction about catechumens versus sinners. It lacks the systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping, numbered degree-structures, or impersonal cosmological exposition that mark the oldest teaching substrate. Even where terms like “light”, “throne”, and “great fire” appear, they function within an ethical/institutional contrast (catechumen vs sinner) rather than as a self-contained cosmological architecture.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Strong hagiographic/dialogue frame: catechumen questions the “apostle”, ‘my master’, page marker, recollection of prior lessons ‘written … in the books’. The content is embedded in Q&A apparatus and institutional categories (catechumens/sinners), indicating editorial compilation layer rather than substrate exposition.
Formulaic transition ‘Then the lord speaks’ and summary of ‘two lessons’. This is pure narratorial linkage typical of the Kephalaia frame.

Direct audience address and exhortation (‘Now, listen … I will recount to you … proclaim to you’) signals application/instruction voice, introducing an institutional teaching about catechumens in transmigration rather than impersonal cosmological mechanics.

Extended moral-educational analogy drawn from ordinary social life (educating children vs servants; rebuke, blows, prison, chains). This is cosmos→contemporary-life illustration, not correspondential mapping internal to the cosmic system; thus a pastoral/application layer.

Despite occasional cosmological vocabulary (‘throne in the light’, ‘great fire’), the paragraph is structured around institutional categories (catechumens/sinners) and their punitive ‘education’. The cosmic terms serve an eschatological threat/hope applied to community members, not a systematic substrate description.

Benedictory/paraenetic closing (‘Blessed are you catechumens … chosen and ordained … their end is loss’) is institutional address and moral outcome language, characteristic of later community exhortation rather than the impersonal teaching core.
